sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2 (CLN2) is a genetic disease caused by deficiency of the enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1), resulting in seizures, vision/cognitive decline, and early death. Cerliponase alfa is an enzyme replacement therapy approved as treatment for CLN2 disease, administered by intracerebroventricular infusion via a surgically implanted device. Maintaining sterility for prolonged scalp-based infusions can be difficult in children and damage devices. We report the development of a technique connecting the intraventricular device and catheter to a chest port to mitigate some of these challenges.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We describe a seven-patient cohort who underwent implantation of our modified infusion system connecting a ventricular catheter distally to a central venous access device (CVAD) port implanted in the anterior chest.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between March 2019 and April 2024, seven (n = 7) patients aged 2–19 years underwent the placement of this system or had an old device converted to a CVAD port system. None of our patients has experienced significant access issues, infection, or required revision since implantation.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The use of an intraventricular access device connected to a CVAD allows for safe and efficacious long-term infusion of cerliponase alfa therapy and provides a more stable and well-tolerated alternative to scalp-based infusions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2 (CLN2) disease, a form of Batten disease, is a rare, autosomal recessive, pediatric neurodegenerative disorder resulting from pathogenic variants in the TPP1 gene encoding the lysosomal enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1) [1]. Deficiency of TPP1 leads to lysosomal accumulation of undegraded proteins, leading to cellular injury and neurodegeneration [1]. CLN2 disease is characterized by seizures, vision loss, and psychomotor regression. In late infantile CLN2 disease, the onset occurs between age 2 and 4 years and includes language delay, refractory epilepsy, ataxia, vision loss, and rapid cognitive/motor decline [2]. Disease progression leads to death by the age of 8 to 12 years [3].

Cerliponase alfa (tradename Brineura, BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc., Novato, CA), a recombinant form of human TPP1 enzyme, is the only approved treatment for CLN2 disease [1]. This drug is also the first approved enzyme replacement therapy administered via extended duration intracerebroventricular (ICV) infusion [4]. FDA-approved in 2017 for patients 3 years of age and older, Brineura has been shown to be safe and effective at slowing the motor and language decline and increasing survival in affected individuals [2, 5].

ICV infusion allows drug administration directly into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via an implanted ventricular access device (VAD) [4]. Typically, these include an implanted ventricular catheter surgically placed into the lateral ventricle by an experienced pediatric neurosurgeon and connected to a subcutaneous reservoir placed under the scalp. The reservoir is then accessible via needle puncture for CSF sampling and administration of intraventricular therapeutic agents. This enzyme administration is required every 2 weeks for the duration of the patient’s life, and each infusion of Brineura lasts approximately 4.5 h [6, 7]. This makes treatment burdensome for patients and families, particularly in young children with seizures for whom maintaining sterile technique during prolonged infusion times through the scalp is very difficult. In addition, degradation of the device reservoir occurs after approximately 105 punctures (4 years of regular administration of Brineura), necessitating access device replacement [8]. Other reported VAD-associated complications include CSF infection, surgical site swelling preventing infusion, leakage or wound breakdown, and catheter obstruction [9].

An alternative infusion system was first described in 2020 by author W. Bruce Cherny on this paper [9]. A standard ventricular catheter with or without a scalp reservoir is instead connected via tunneled shunt tubing to a CVAD implanted subcutaneously in the anterior chest. This approach combines two techniques familiar to neurosurgeons—shunt catheter tubing implantation and subcutaneous pocket creation (such as in placement of a vagal nerve stimulator battery). However, in this case, the implant is a chest port for drug infusion.

Here we describe seven patients from our institutions who underwent this modified surgical approach to reduce the difficulty of prolonged scalp-based infusions. Our conversion of the traditional scalp port to a chest port was able to be performed with ease and has resulted in better quality of life for these patients, with no reported adverse reactions or complications since implantation.

sec.title: Case series
sec.p:
Patient 1, an 11-year-old male, received an early diagnosis for late infantile CLN2 disease at age 2. In 2016, he underwent placement of a traditional VAD at an outside facility and began receiving Brineura infusions. After relocating to Idaho, he began to have difficulty with these infusions over time, often requiring multiple needle sticks to access his scalp reservoir. A post-infusion CSF leak occurred after approximately 80 accesses of his system, necessitating system revision. In 2019, he underwent removal of his VAD and replacement with the modified port system we describe. Since implantation, his device has been accessed over 162 times without infection, device failure, or infusion issues. A photo of his explanted VAD can be found in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
Explanted ventricular access device reservoir from Patient 1, showing shear damage caused by frequent, repeated access attempts with a needle

Patient 2, an 8-year-old female, was diagnosed with late infantile CLN2 disease in the few months prior to placement of her access device at the age of 4. She originally presented with new onset intractable epilepsy, followed by several months of motor regression. She was developmentally normal up to that point with a normal birth history. Her symptoms ultimately raised suspicion for a neurodevelopmental disorder and inpatient screening labs and molecular testing confirmed the diagnosis. She was urgently referred to Biochemical Genetics and Neurosurgery clinics for management, and she underwent port placement 1 week later in 2020. Her port has since been accessed over 100 times without complication.

Patient 3, a 24-year-old male with atypical CLN2 disease, presented more gradually with cognitive delays noted at age 2–3 years, incoordination noted at age 5, dyslexia at age 7, and ataxia at age 14. He was diagnosed with atypical CLN2 at 18 years old via enzyme level and genetic testing. He underwent VAD placement with cranial access in 2019 at an outside hospital (OSH), with subsequent access difficulties on multiple occasions leading to multiple access attempts for infusions, as well as a diagnosed P. acnes infection managed conservatively at the OSH. His symptoms have been slowly progressive while on Brineura treatment, and given concerns about his scalp reservoir, he was recommended for revision to this new system, which he underwent in late 2020 at Seattle Children’s Hospital (SCH) [6]. His port has been accessed 140 times without complication.

Patient 4, a 19-year-old female and sibling of Patient 3, also had prior diagnosis of atypical CLN2 and a VAD implantation. She was originally noted to have failure to thrive and developmental delay in infancy, as well as cyclical vomiting. She presented with speech and motor delay with first words and walking around 15 months of age, ultimately requiring an individualized education program and speech therapy. She was diagnosed with atypical CLN2 at age 14 via enzyme testing after her brother’s diagnosis and was confirmed to harbor the known familial variants. She did not have any seizures, vision loss, or motor/cognitive regression prior to starting treatment. She had no access problems or subsequent complications of the procedure and stable symptoms since beginning Brineura infusions but given the opportunity to convert her system to a chest port with greater ease of access, her parents requested a revision. This occurred the same day as her sibling’s revision. Her port has been accessed 110 times without complication.

Patient 5, a 7-year-old male with atypical CLN2 disease, was first noted to have developmental delays at 18 months of age, with delayed speech, and “staring spells” at age 3 that were diagnosed as absence seizures. His seizure workup revealed a TPP1 genetic variant and low TPP1 enzyme activity, for which he was referred to the SCH Biochemical Genetics Clinic. He underwent placement of a chest port access system in late 2023. He has had no access problems or complications associated with the procedure. His symptoms have remained well-controlled, and he has tolerated the infusions well. His port has been accessed 41 times without complication.

Patient 6, a 3-year-old male and sibling of Patient 4, was diagnosed with atypical CLN2 disease with molecular and enzyme testing after his brother tested positive for the disease. He presented with speech delay at 22 months of age. He underwent a placement of a chest port access system in late 2023. He has had no access problems or complications associated with the procedure. His port has been accessed 40 times to date without complication.

Patient 7, a 5-year-old male, was diagnosed with late infantile CLN2 disease and presented with seizures, speech delay, and tics first noticed at age 3. He was found to harbor mutations in TPP1, with absent enzyme activity. He underwent placement of a chest port access system early this year. He has since been accessed 30 times at our institution without any complications.

sec.title: Modification of surgical approach
sec.p: After the induction of general anesthesia, the bed is rotated to facilitate exposure of the head and chest wall. The patient is registered to real-time intraoperative surgical navigation for optimal ventricular catheter placement. A trajectory for the ventricular catheter is planned with the distal tip situated in the frontal horn near the foramen of Monro. The hair is clipped, and the scalp, neck, and chest are cleaned and prepped in sterile fashion. An incision is made in the scalp near the planned entry point, and dermis and galea are opened. A subgaleal pocket is made along the planned trajectory of the distal catheter, similar to a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt procedure.

A burr hole is made at the planned entry point, and the underlying dura is coagulated and opened. Hemostasis is achieved, and using intraoperative navigation, an antibiotic impregnated ventricular catheter is passed to the appropriate depth with visualization of CSF efflux. This is connected to a Rickham reservoir which is secured to the pericranium and tied to the ventricular catheter.

The location for the distal port access device is opened, and the subcutaneous tissue is dissected until a pocket is formed in the epifascial or subfascial plane depending on the patient’s body habitus. A shunt tunneler is passed from the scalp to the chest port pocket in similar fashion to a VP shunt. An antibiotic impregnated distal catheter is passed down the tract to the chest pocket. The tunneler is removed, and the distal catheter is cut to size. The catheter can be left long with redundant looping if there is the likelihood for significant growth of the patient over time. A CVAD (in our cases, a PowerPort™ Slim Implantable Port with 6-French side port, Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD), Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) is connected to the distal catheter and secured with a silk tie. The PowerPort™ Slim Implantable Port is a small chest port measures 1.8 cm in diameter with a height/profile of 8 mm and a weight of 8.9 g. The port is secured to the fascia or loose connective tissue in the proper orientation for access (Fig. 2). It should be noted that we used a port with an open 6 French side inlet. Some CVADs come standard with a catheter already integrated and attached, which is less desirable as it would require an additional straight connector to connect to the shunt tubing.Fig. 2
Illustrated representation of novel chest port to ventricular access device

At this point, multiple access tests are performed to ensure the system is functional and to determine the volume of CSF contained within the Rickham reservoir and distal system. This is documented for future drug administration procedures and in our experience is typically around 1.5 mL. The wounds are thoroughly irrigated and closed in anatomic layers.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: CLN2 disease is a fatal, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative condition. Clinical outcomes are improved with early diagnosis and treatment with enzyme replacement therapy [1]. Cerliponase alpha intraventricular infusion has drastically changed the landscape of treatment for patients with this disease, slowing the motor and language decline and extending lifespan with consistent therapy [4, 5]. However, therapy with intraventricular infusion is not without difficulty.

Among reported cohorts treated with infusions via VADs, there are high rates of patients requiring surgical revision of their devices due to issues related to infection or device failure. One study reviewing survival of VADs for CLN2 treatment in 17 patients noted device related complications in nearly half of implanted VADs, with over 1/3 requiring revision, and a median survival time of 301 days in catheters that required revision [10]. This is similar to other cohorts that have reported high revision rates due to infection or reservoir damage, sometimes approaching 50% of patients who ultimately need revision of their reservoirs [11]. In children, this represents a costly and disruptive burden as patients and families must make arrangements that disrupt work or educational activities and subject patients to further anesthetic and surgical risks should they need to undergo device revision or replacement.

Infection risk in this patient cohort may be higher than in patients with VADs in place for other forms of medical management, such as those receiving intraventricular chemotherapy [12]. Given the repeated and long-term dosing necessary to treat CLN2 via intraventricular infusion, patients will live their lives with multiple needle sticks for frequent device access. Despite stringent aseptic technique for device access, the necessity of repeated taps over the course of treatment increases risks for shearing of access ports by needles, as was the case in Patient 1’s original VAD (Fig. 1), and for introducing infection over time [1, 10]. This risk is magnified by the underlying patient population, as patients with CLN2 are recommended to begin therapy as soon as possible following diagnosis, often during early childhood. Ensuring sterile technique for scalp access throughout the duration of the required multiple-hour infusion protocol in young children is a daunting task and is likely a large part of these devices showing higher rates of device-related complications than those for other types of therapies [12]. Additionally, patients with neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are at higher risk of anesthetic complications, making the prospect of device revision under general anesthesia all the more burdensome for families and providers [2].

Our novel approach of connecting the VAD to a chest-based CVAD infusion system (Figs. 2 and 3) allows much easier device access and appears to be much better tolerated by patients in our experience thus far. With a traditional scalp-based system, stabilizing a needle in the scalp requires an extensive head dressing in order to ensure stability in a relatively shallow scalp reservoir, and long infusion times make access and stabilization difficult with very young patients who frequently move about. In contrast, a chest port-based system is inherently more stable due to the larger and deeper port design and more subcutaneous tissue between the port and skin to hold the needle. It can be stabilized much easier using traditional chest port access methods with transparent dressings that allow for better needle visualization throughout the infusion. This method generally allows for greater patient mobility as well (Tables 1 and 2).Fig. 3

Although the device provides significant benefit to the patient as described in our series, there are some limitations that are device specific. Compared to traditional VAD such as the Ommaya reservoir, the PowerPort™ Slim Implantable Port or similar device may have a slight increased cost, particularly if the healthcare institution does not have a specific contract for the device already. The device is also slightly smaller and of different configuration compared to traditional VAD; therefore, there may be a learning curve for providers who are not familiar with port access but have experience with VAD access. By utilizing a chest port location, this increases the length of tubing required to go from the reservoir to the ventricle. As stated in the surgical procedure description, this dead space is estimated to be approximately 1.5 mL. In a traditional VAD infusion for cerliponase alfa, approximately 10 mL of CSF is removed prior to 300 mg or 10 mL infusion of the medication. For our series of patients, to address the additional “dead space,” we remove approximately 11.5 mL of CSF, administer 10 mL of the medication over the 4- to 5-h infusion window, and then an additional 2-mL “flush” of sterile saline is used to ensure complete drug delivery.

We describe seven patients undergoing modified port placement for infusions at our institutions. So far, none of these patients has required revision due to device failure or infection, with over 3 years of follow-up in more than half. Combined, these ports have been accessed over 450 times since implantation, and our patients with the longest follow-up have gone > 1900 days without device failure. These devices appear to be better tolerated and to have improved durability compared to traditional scalp-based access methods [10].

This approach has the potential for more secure access during prolonged infusion. This, combined with the sturdy structural design of the central venous access devices as the primary access site, decreases the chances of needle shear causing access port degradation and, in our experience, has shown low rates of device failure related to infection as well. However, further long-term follow-up and broad experience with additional patients are needed to fully compare this modality with classical scalp-based access systems, and currently, this application of CVADs is an off-label use.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This case series represents the first published experience of a modified surgical approach for implantation of a VAD for management of CLN2 disease utilizing a chest-based central venous access port site for intraventricular infusion. While additional patient data and follow-up is needed to better compare this approach with the typical scalp-based reservoir locations discussed in the literature, this approach has the potential to reduce rates of device failure and infection while making the process of prolonged cerliponase alpha infusions easier and safer for patients, families, and providers.
